entities.name: Athenian Assembly
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Athenian Ekklesia (Assembly) was the primary governing body of direct democracy in ancient Athens during its classical period (508-322 BCE). Open to all male citizens over 18, the Assembly met regularly on the Pnyx hill to debate and vote on laws, foreign policy, war, treaties, and public officials — creating the world's first functioning democracy and establishing concepts still fundamental to democratic theory.

Cleisthenes' reforms of 508-507 BCE created the institutional structure: 10 new tribes replacing the four traditional phyle, creating a mixed citizen body that broke up aristocratic clan power. The Assembly, together with the Council of 500 (Boule) selected by lot, and the popular law courts (dikasteria), constituted Athenian demokratia. At its height, 6,000-8,000 citizens could participate in Assembly meetings on the Pnyx, though meetings of 40 per year typically saw smaller numbers.

Pericles' 'Funeral Oration' (431 BCE), recorded by Thucydides, articulated democracy's philosophical principles: 'We are called a democracy, for the administration is in the hands of the many and not of the few.' The assembly voted for the Sicilian Expedition (415 BCE) — a catastrophic decision killing 40,000 Athenian men — demonstrating both democracy's decisiveness and its vulnerability to demagogic persuasion. Democratic Athens produced Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle, who debated democracy's merits and limitations in texts still studied today.
